template.familyBody:
Bonjour {name},

Notre enfant a récemment reçu le diagnostic {condition}. Nous vous avons trouvés grâce au Rare Disease Atlas.

{why}

Nous serions heureux d'échanger avec d'autres familles et de connaître les études ou registres auxquels nous pourrions participer. Pouvez-vous nous dire comment vous contacter ?

Merci,
[Votre nom]
template.groupBody:
Bonjour {name},

Je dirige un groupe de patients pour {condition}. Nous pensons que nos communautés partagent un problème dans le corps.

{why}

Nous aimerions parler de ce que chacun a construit et de ce que nous pourrions partager, pour que les familles des deux groupes en profitent. Des experts devraient vérifier ce lien avant tout projet.

Pourrions-nous nous rencontrer 30 minutes dans les prochaines semaines ?

Bien cordialement,
[Votre nom]
template.note: C'est un modèle simple. Avec le serveur de l'atlas, le brouillon est écrit à partir des enregistrements liés, puis vérifié.

about.title: About Zebratlas
about.lead: Zebratlas helps families and patient groups with a rare genetic condition find the people who can help.
about.how: We connect public records: disease and gene databases, study registries, research grants, papers and the websites of patient organisations. Every connection shows where it comes from and when we checked it.
about.limits: It gives no medical advice and does not judge treatments. It can miss groups and studies, especially outside English-language sources. When we find nothing, we say so and show where we looked.
about.help: Patient groups, registries and researchers can add what we are missing. We check every submission before it appears.
about.who: Zebratlas started at the 7th Global AI Hackathon (Hack-Nation, challenge 5). The code is open source.

sources.lead: Everything Zebratlas shows comes from these sources. Each entry names its licence, the version we use and the attribution the source asks for.
sources.code: Our own code is open source. The licence of a source applies to the data taken from it.

use.orphanet: Rare diseases, their genes, how common they are and when they start.
use.hpo: Signs and symptoms, so conditions with the same signs can be compared.
use.mondo: One name and code per disease, across all the other databases.
use.g2p: Which gene changes cause which conditions, and how the change acts.
use.clingen: How strong the evidence is that a gene causes a condition.
use.hgnc: Official gene names and their other names.
use.go: What each gene does in the cell, to find conditions that break the same process.
use.reactome: The processes in the body that genes work in together.
use.clinvar: Which exact gene changes are known to cause disease.
use.ctgov: Studies and registries, whether they take people, and their official contacts.
use.reporter: Research grants: who works on which gene.
use.pubmed: Who publishes on which gene. We keep only the bibliographic details.
use.wikidata: Names of conditions in many languages.
use.orgs: Patient groups: their name, country, language and contact route.

partners.lead: Zebratlas has no formal partners yet.
partners.text: We would like to work with patient organisations, registries and research networks: to keep their entries correct and to connect the data they hold. If that is you, tell us what you have.

contact.medical: We cannot answer medical questions. Please ask your doctor.
contact.a11y: We aim to meet WCAG 2.2 at level AA. If something does not work for you, or you have feedback of any kind, write to us at the address above.

privacy.lead: You can use Zebratlas without an account and without being tracked.
privacy.none: We use no analytics, no advertising and no tracking cookies. We do not sell or share data.
privacy.account: We store your e-mail address, an optional display name, a secured form of your password and what you save. One cookie keeps you signed in. You can delete your account and everything in it at any time.
privacy.contributeTitle: If you send us a correction or data
privacy.contribute: We store what you send and, if you give them, your name and contact address, so a reviewer can ask back. Accepted contributions are shown with their source, not with your contact details.
privacy.language: When you paste or upload a document, our server removes obvious identifiers before finding search terms. The notice beside the search box names any processor that may receive the text, before you send it. Documents are processed in memory and deleted afterwards. We keep only a fingerprint, size and timing. If you sign in and choose to save a document, it is encrypted in your account; you can view, download or delete it on Your data. We never send messages for you.
privacy.logs: Our server briefly records technical data such as IP addresses to protect the service from abuse.
privacy.rights: Under the GDPR you can ask what we store about you, have it corrected or deleted, and complain to a data protection authority.

about.title: Comment ça marche
about.lead: L'atlas met en relation les familles et les groupes de patients avec les personnes et les études qui peuvent les aider. Chaque lien montre d'où il vient.
about.s1Text: Nous réunissons les grands catalogues de maladies (MONDO, Orphanet, OMIM, HPO) en un enregistrement par maladie, en gardant chaque identifiant source.
about.s2Text: Groupes de patients, études, registres, chercheurs, articles et subventions sont liés aux maladies. Chaque lien garde son enregistrement source, la date et une empreinte.
about.s3Text: Les modèles de langage écrivent les phrases simples et les brouillons uniquement à partir d'enregistrements liés. Un validateur vérifie que chaque phrase cite un enregistrement.
about.s4Title: Des problèmes communs, pas seulement des noms
about.s4Text: Les maladies sont regroupées selon le gène et le processus dans le corps, puis selon les signes typiques. Les maladies qui se ressemblent mais ont une autre cause sont signalées.
about.s5Title: Dans le monde entier et en de nombreuses langues
about.s5Text: Des sources dans toutes les langues sont trouvées, traduites et reliées à la même maladie. Le texte original est toujours conservé.
about.s6Text: Le code, le traitement des données et l'export du graphe sont ouverts. Le README du dépôt donne une seule commande pour tout lancer.
about.privacyText: Vous n'avez pas besoin de compte. Nous n'enregistrons pas vos recherches et nous ne vendons jamais de données.

design.assay: Ask a domain expert to select a quantitative assay of {pathway} and check that it measures the relevant function in both conditions.
design.controls: Compare models with verified variants from both conditions against matched corrected controls. Randomize batches and blind the analysis.
design.rescue: Include a control that changes the selected pathway and a correction or rescue condition for each disease model. Check cell health to distinguish pathway effects from nonspecific damage.
design.strata: Analyze each condition and group of variant effects separately before comparing effects and rescue responses.

validate.annotation: A pathway annotation does not establish a shared disease mechanism or treatment response.
validate.models: An expert must select a specific pathway measurement, relevant cell type and verified models for the variants. Check whether these models are available.
validate.plan: After estimating variation in a pilot, pre-register effect direction and decision criteria. Plan independent biological replicates and sample size with a statistician.
validate.effects: Check each variant's effect and inheritance before combining condition groups. Analyze opposite effects in separate groups.
validate.findings: Review uncertainty findings linked to these conditions before interpreting a shared assay.

proposal.question: Test whether variants associated with {conditions} disrupt the same measurable function in {pathway}.
proposal.support: Both condition models show the planned pathway change compared with controls, and correction restores the same measurement in both. Replicate the result independently.
proposal.challenge: Only one condition changes the measurement, effects point in incompatible directions, or differences disappear after accounting for cell health or batch.

trail.s3: STXBP1 and SNAP25 affect machinery that brain cells use to send signals. Some gene changes affect that machinery differently. Both communities are included in Simons Searchlight; ask its study team about joining or reusing research resources.
trail.s5: Release of signals between brain cells
trail.s6: This is an infrastructure-reuse opportunity, not evidence of treatment benefit.
trail.s7: Same process does not mean the same defect: some SNAP25 and STXBP1 variants increase release instead of reducing it. Variants must be compared separately before any shared approach.
trail.s8: The SNAP25 condition has conflicting names and codes in the catalogues; we link the gene community, not one disease code.
trail.s9: Joining from outside the USA is possible, but blood collection there is reviewed case by case. Available samples and cell lines are unknown until the team answers.
trail.s12: The study record and the official programme both name its study coordinator as the contact for joining and for research access.
trail.s13: STXBP1 and SNAP25 communities: reusing Simons Searchlight for a variant-stratified comparison
trail.s14:
Hello Simons Searchlight study team,

We are exploring a research comparison between the STXBP1 and SNAP25 communities, both listed in Simons Searchlight. Experimental studies show that variants can affect synaptic release differently, so we would separate variants before considering a shared approach.

Could your team advise whether an investigator can reuse your data collection and access process for this comparison, which data and samples are available, and who could discuss feasibility with us? We would also like to confirm country, language and variant eligibility before inviting families.

Thank you,
[Your name]
[Your patient group]
trail.s15: Do selected STXBP1 and SNAP25 variants share the same defect in how brain cells release signals?
trail.s16: If they do, one line of research could serve both communities.
trail.s20: Release of signals between brain cells
trail.s21: STXBP1 C180Y lowered the amount of the protein in mouse neurons (protein instability).
trail.s22: SNAP25 I67N destabilised the release machinery and reduced spontaneous and evoked release in neurons.
trail.s23: SNAP25 V48F and D166Y increase spontaneous release instead of reducing it.
trail.s24: STXBP1 L446F (two homozygous cases) increased evoked transmission in a neuronal model.
trail.s25: With one normal STXBP1 copy present, measured transmission was normal in the same C180Y study.
trail.s26: Whether any rescue works for both genotypes: no experiment yet.
trail.s27: Which matched cell lines and samples are available, and which lab would run it.
trail.s28: Compare STXBP1 C180Y with separately specified SNAP25 variants (I67N kept apart from V48F/D166Y) in matched neurons with one protocol: spontaneous and evoked release, readily releasable pool, synchronisation; isogenic controls, independent cultures, blinded analysis. A defect in opposite directions blocks pooling.
trail.s29: Proposed design; feasibility and power still to be worked out.
trail.s30: Ask the Simons Searchlight study team whether its collection supports a variant-stratified STXBP1/SNAP25 comparison.
trail.s31: Simons Searchlight is recruiting; its conditions include STXBP1 Encephalopathy With Epilepsy and SNAP25; the study coordinator is the central contact.
trail.s32: Existing data and biospecimens can be requested through SFARI Base after review.
trail.s33: Simons Searchlight studies the SNAP25 community.
trail.s34: Official contact page of the programme.
trail.s35: STXBP1 patient variants such as C180Y reduce protein amount; experiments support protein instability.
trail.s36: A homozygous STXBP1 variant (L446F) increased evoked transmission in a neuronal model: not every variant reduces release.
trail.s37: SNAP25 takes part in vesicle fusion; I67N reduced release, while V48F and D166Y increased spontaneous release.
trail.s38: Families outside the USA can join; blood collection outside the USA is reviewed individually.
trail.s39: The programme is a natural-history database and biorepository, not a treatment trial.
trail.s40: G2P maps the SNAP25 disorder to MONDO:0014590, whose MONDO name is congenital myasthenic syndrome 18: an unresolved naming conflict.
trail.s41: A published series describes 23 people with SNAP25 variants; it mixes new and previously reported individuals, so they must not be added to other cohorts as independent cases.
